modules.title: Problem Formulation
modules.description: Assess how the problem was defined and whether AI is the appropriate solution.

questions.text: Have you compared AI with simpler options such as a statistical model, rules or a manual process?
questions.expectedPractice: Before building, you compare AI with at least one simpler method and one non-computational option on expected performance, cost, the skills and infrastructure each needs to keep running, and the risks to the people affected, and record your choice and why.
questions.whyAsked: AI that rules or a manual process could match still costs money, power and upkeep, and its errors fall on the people it serves.
evidenceExamples: a C-01 alternatives analysis, filled in
the protocol section with the comparison
minutes of the meeting where you made the choice

answerPrompts.done: Name the options compared, what decided it and where the choice is recorded.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the options compared so far and those still to compare.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you plan to compare, or what is blocking it.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no comparison applies; this is unusual here.

questions.text: Have you defined the problem, its objectives and its success criteria?
questions.expectedPractice: Your written problem statement names who has the problem, the decision or task the system will support, and checkable success: the measure, your target and what would count as not good enough.
questions.whyAsked: Without a written problem statement, nobody can later tell whether the system helped, and work drifts towards whatever the data allows.
evidenceExamples: the problem statement in the protocol or concept note
a one-page project brief with objectives and success measures
minutes of the meeting where you agreed the objectives

answerLabels.partly: Partly, some of it is defined

answerPrompts.done: State the problem, who it affects, your success measures and where the full statement is kept; this prints in the data card and model card.
answerPrompts.partly: State the problem and the measures defined so far, then what is still open; this prints in the data card and model card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: State the problem as you see it now and when you will define it; this prints in the data card and model card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why this system needs no problem statement; this prints in the data card and model card.

questions.text: Have you identified everyone the system affects, directly or indirectly?
questions.expectedPractice: You list the groups the system affects and how it affects each: those who use its outputs, those the outputs are about, those whose data trains it, and others who carry its costs or benefits.
questions.whyAsked: Nobody plans for harms to groups left off the list, and later questions on groups, consent and consultation build on it.
evidenceExamples: a stakeholder list or map in the protocol
a C-07 stakeholder impact map, filled in
notes from a meeting where you reviewed the list

answerLabels.not_applicable: No list of those affected applies

answerPrompts.done: Users first, name each group by role or category, never as individuals, how it is affected and where the list is kept; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.partly: Users first, name the groups listed so far by role, never as individuals, and those still missing; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Name the users you expect, by role, never as individuals, and when you will list the rest; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no list of those affected applies to this project; this prints in the model card.

questions.text: Have you assessed effects on protected or vulnerable groups, for example by gender, age, ethnicity, disability or income?
questions.expectedPractice: You name the groups who could be harmed or left out where the system is used, including locally marginalised groups, and record for each how the system could affect it and what you will check or change.
questions.whyAsked: AI harms fall most often on groups already disadvantaged and least present in the data, and which groups depends on the setting.
evidenceExamples: the group effects section of the protocol or C-02 assessment
notes from a consultation with group representatives
a written analysis of effects by group

answerPrompts.done: Name each group, its main effect, your response to the largest risk and where it is recorded. Describe groups, never individuals; upload no records about them.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the groups assessed and those still to assess. Describe groups, never individuals, and upload no records about them.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you will assess this, or what is blocking it.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no group assessment applies to this project.

questions.text: Have you assessed the system's impact on human rights?
questions.expectedPractice: In proportion to the risk, you assess how the system could affect people's rights, such as privacy, fair treatment, access to services and the chance to challenge a decision: a short written note for a low-stakes tool, a fuller assessment for a system that decides about people.
questions.whyAsked: Some harms, such as a lost chance to appeal or a withheld service, fall on everyone the system touches; this question asks about those rights, and a separate question asks about particular groups.
evidenceExamples: the rights assessment, or its section of the C-02 assessment
an ethics committee's comments on rights
the decision note on changes made

answerPrompts.done: Name the rights you assessed, what you found and changed, any reviewer by role and where it is recorded; for a short note, say why the risk is low.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the rights assessed so far and those still to assess.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you will assess this, or what is blocking it.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no rights assessment applies, not even a short note.

questions.text: Have you checked which perspectives the problem needs (disciplines, lived experience, gender, language and culture of those affected) and brought in those your team lacks?
questions.expectedPractice: You list the perspectives the problem needs, compare them with your team and fill the gaps, for example with a domain adviser, a community representative or a reviewer from another discipline. The list says who fills each gap, by role, and how they take part.
questions.whyAsked: A team whose members share one background misses the same things, so it needs to know which perspectives are missing and bring them in, for example through multi-stakeholder consultation.
evidenceExamples: the perspectives list
terms of reference for an advisory group
notes from a review by an outside adviser

answerLabels.done: Yes, we checked and filled any gaps

answerPrompts.done: Name any missing perspectives, who now provides each by role, and where the list is kept. Record no one's gender, nationality or other personal details.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the gaps filled, by role, and those still open. Record no one's personal details.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Name the perspectives you lack and how you plan to bring them in. Record no one's personal details.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why checking for missing perspectives does not apply to this problem.

questions.text: Have you estimated the system's energy use and carbon cost?
questions.expectedPractice: Before building, you estimate the computing and energy that training and running need, for example from hardware hours times power draw or with CodeCarbon, weigh them against the expected benefit, and record the estimate and your choice.
questions.whyAsked: Large models use energy and money that small projects and unreliable grids can ill afford; an early estimate leaves time to choose a lighter method.
evidenceExamples: the estimate in the protocol or C-02 assessment
a CodeCarbon summary file
a note comparing the energy use of two candidate methods

answerLabels.partly: Partly, for some of the work

answerPrompts.done: Give the computing hours and energy, the method, your choice and where the estimate is kept; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.partly: Give what you have estimated so far and what is still missing; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Give the computing you expect and when you will estimate it; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why the system needs no estimate of computing or energy; this prints in the model card.

modules.title: Data Collection & Preparation
modules.description: Assess the quality, representativeness, and ethical handling of your data.

questions.text: Have you recorded your data's sources, how they were collected and why you chose them?
questions.expectedPractice: For each source, you record where the data came from, who collected it, how and when, and why you chose it, and keep the record with the data, such as a datasheet, so an outsider could judge its fit for the use.
questions.whyAsked: Without a record of how the data was gathered, nobody can judge its fit, repeat the work or see its limits.
evidenceExamples: a datasheet for the dataset (C-19)
an issued data card from this platform
the data collection section of the protocol
a link to the data-access agreement

answerPrompts.done: Say why the data was gathered, then its sources, methods, period and setting; this prints in the data card. Link the datasheet, never the data itself.
answerPrompts.partly: Say why the data was gathered, what is recorded so far and what is not; this prints in the data card. Never upload the data itself.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say why the data is being gathered, what you know of its sources and when you will record them; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why the project uses no data source; this prints in the data card.

questions.text: Have you checked whether your data represents the population the system will serve?
questions.expectedPractice: You compare your data's make-up with the population it will serve, group by group (such as sex, age, district, language, rural or urban), using a source such as census or clinic figures, and record under-represented groups and what you did.
questions.whyAsked: A model learns the population in its data, not the one it serves, so thin groups get worse results nobody notices without a comparison.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-05 notebook
a table comparing the data and the population by group
the representativeness section of the protocol

answerPrompts.done: Give the make-up by group and place in counts, never records, then the gaps, what you did and where it is kept; this prints in the data card and model card.
answerPrompts.partly: Give the make-up checked so far and the groups still to check, in counts, never records; this prints in the data card and model card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Give what you know of the make-up so far, in counts, never records, and your plan; this prints in the data card and model card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no population comparison applies; this prints in the data card and model card.

questions.text: Have you checked whether any input could stand in for a sensitive attribute (for example, village for ethnicity), and decided what to do?
questions.expectedPractice: You check which inputs could stand in for a sensitive attribute in your setting, such as village for ethnicity or phone type for income, test how strongly they are linked where you have the data, and record for each whether you keep, remove or monitor it.
questions.whyAsked: Removing a sensitive attribute does not stop a model using it when another input, such as place, language or name, carries the same information.
evidenceExamples: the output of a check on links between variables
a decision note listing possible stand-in variables and choices
the feature list with notes

answerPrompts.done: Say first whether the model uses or predicts a sensitive attribute, then the inputs checked, how, your choices and where they are recorded; this prints in the model card. Record no one's attributes.
answerPrompts.partly: Say whether the model uses or predicts a sensitive attribute, then the checks done and still to do; this prints in the model card. Record no one's attributes.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say whether the model uses or predicts a sensitive attribute, and your plan; this prints in the model card. Record no one's attributes.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say whether the model uses or predicts a sensitive attribute, and why no check for stand-ins applies; this prints in the model card.

questions.text: Have you checked that labels are correct and consistent?
questions.expectedPractice: You write labelling guidelines, have a share of items labelled twice, measure how often labellers agree, and resolve or record disagreements; for labels from routine records, you check a sample against the source. You set and record the share and the agreement you accept.
questions.whyAsked: A model is no better than its labels, and when one site or language is labelled differently, its people bear the errors.
evidenceExamples: the labelling guidelines
the agreement summary from the C-04 notebook
a note on how disagreements were resolved

answerPrompts.done: Say how labels were assigned and by whom, by role; this prints in the data card. Attach the agreement results.
answerPrompts.partly: Say how labels were assigned and by whom, by role, which checks are done and which remain; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say how labels are assigned and by whom, by role, and when you will check them; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why the data has no labels to check; this prints in the data card.

questions.text: Does your data contain information that could identify a person, or other sensitive personal information?
questions.expectedPractice: You check every field and file you will hold, including free text, images and audio, for anything that could identify a person directly or in combination with other data, and record the answer.
questions.whyAsked: Personal data brings duties of consent and protection, and data can identify a person through a combination, such as a village, an age and a rare condition.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say which data you checked, field by field or file by file, and what you found, describing kinds of data and never copying personal data. Your answer prints in the data card and model card; if you answer not sure, say what you still need to check.
evidenceExamples: a data inventory saying for each field whether it can identify a person
the data protection section of the protocol

questions.text: Have you obtained proper informed consent to collect and use the data?
questions.expectedPractice: You tell the people whose data you use, in a language and form they understand, what it is for, that it may be used to build an AI system, who will use it, how long it is kept and how to withdraw, and they agree to the uses now planned. Where others collected the data or an ethics committee waived consent, you hold the record of that.
questions.whyAsked: Consent for one purpose does not automatically cover training a model, and uses beyond it can stop the work and lose the trust of those who shared the data.
evidenceExamples: a blank consent form and information sheet
the ethics approval letter, or the waiver, or its reference
the consent clause of a data-access agreement

answerLabels.done: Yes, consent or a waiver covers it
answerLabels.partly: Partly, not for every use or person
answerLabels.not_applicable: No consent or waiver is needed

answerPrompts.done: Say how consent was obtained, in which languages and whether it covers AI and sharing, or the waiving committee and reference; this prints in the data card. Attach the blank form, never signed ones.
answerPrompts.partly: Say how consent was obtained and which uses or people it does not yet cover; this prints in the data card. Attach the blank form, never signed ones.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say how you plan to obtain consent (written, oral with a witness, community and individual) and in which languages; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why the data needs neither consent nor a waiver; this prints in the data card.

questions.text: Have you removed or replaced the details in your data that could identify a person (anonymisation or pseudonymisation)?
questions.expectedPractice: Before analysis, you remove or replace direct identifiers and coarsen details that could identify a person in combination, such as exact dates, small villages or rare conditions, then check for anyone who could still be singled out. You keep any key linking codes to people apart from the data, open only to set roles.
questions.whyAsked: Removing names is not enough when a few details together point to one person, and if the data leaks or is shared, no one in it should be recognisable.
evidenceExamples: the de-identification steps in the data management plan
the summary file from the C-10 notebook
a report of a check for people who could be singled out

answerPrompts.done: Say what you removed, replaced or coarsened, how you checked and where it is recorded; this prints in the data card. Say who holds any linking key, by role, never the key itself.
answerPrompts.partly: Say what you have removed, replaced or coarsened so far and what remains; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say how and when you plan to de-identify the data; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why the data needs no de-identification; this prints in the data card.

questions.text: Which listed data quality checks have you run?
questions.expectedPractice: Before training, you run the checks your data needs and record what each found: all eight for most tabular data; for images, text or audio, which do not fit and what you did instead.
questions.whyAsked: Quality problems found after training are far harder to trace; most common are records missing for some places or periods.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-03 notebook
a data-quality report

answerLabels.partly: Some of the checks our data needs

answerPrompts.done: Say what the checks found, where it is recorded and why any unticked check does not fit; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.partly: Say which needed checks are still to do, and why any others do not fit your data; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you will run the checks, or what is blocking them; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no data quality check applies to your data; this prints in the data card.

questions.text: Which listed bias types have you assessed your data for?
questions.expectedPractice: You assess your data for each bias type that fits how it was made and record what you found: for most projects historical, population, sampling, measurement and exclusion; labelling where people assigned labels; survey and survivorship where they apply. You explain each unticked type as not relevant.
questions.whyAsked: Each bias type enters data in its own way, so each needs its own check.
evidenceExamples: the bias assessment notes
the summary file from the C-04 notebook
a data-quality report with a section on bias

answerLabels.done: Every type that fits our data
answerLabels.partly: Some of the types that fit

answerPrompts.done: Say what you found, where it is recorded and why any unticked type does not fit; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.partly: Say which fitting types are still to assess, and why any others do not fit; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you will assess bias, or what is blocking it; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no bias type applies to your data; this prints in the data card.

questions.text: Have you assessed whether your data collection could introduce selection bias?
questions.expectedPractice: You describe how people or records came into the data and who could be missing, such as people without phones, those who do not attend clinics or areas without coverage, and record how you measured or corrected for it.
questions.whyAsked: Data gathered only from people easy to reach leaves out the rest, so the model works least well for those hardest to serve.
evidenceExamples: the sampling section of the protocol
a comparison of who is in the data with who was eligible
a note on corrections made

answerPrompts.done: Say if it is a sample or a full collection, how it was gathered, who could be missed, what you did and where it is recorded; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.partly: Say whether it is a sample or a full collection, what you have assessed and what is still open; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say whether it is a sample or a full collection, how it is gathered and your plan; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no selection-bias check applies to this project; this prints in the data card.

questions.text: Have you checked whether past patterns in your data reflect discrimination or systemic inequity?
questions.expectedPractice: You check whether past decisions in the data, such as who was referred, treated or given credit, were unfair to some groups, and record what you found and any change to the labels, features or use of the model.
questions.whyAsked: A model trained on past decisions repeats them, unfair ones included, and records of who received a service often show access, not need.
evidenceExamples: a written analysis of past patterns by group
notes from a review with domain experts
the decision note on changes made

answerLabels.not_applicable: The data holds no past decisions

answerPrompts.done: Say which past patterns you examined, what you found and changed, and where it is recorded; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.partly: Say which past patterns you have examined and which remain; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say which past patterns you plan to examine, and when; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why the data holds no past decisions about people; this prints in the data card.

questions.text: Have you checked whether your data is recent enough for when the system will be used?
questions.expectedPractice: You record the period your data covers, check what has changed since, such as policies, seasons, outbreaks, prices or devices, and record whether the data still fits the period of use.
questions.whyAsked: Data describes the time it was collected, so a model built on old data may serve a situation that no longer exists.
evidenceExamples: the data description with dates
a note on changes since collection
a comparison of older and recent data

answerPrompts.done: Give the period covered, the changes since that matter, what you did and where it is recorded; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.partly: Give the period the data covers, the changes checked and those still to check; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Give the period the data covers and when you will check for changes; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Give the period the data covers and say why its age does not matter for this use; this prints in the data card.

questions.text: Have you set data governance rules covering access, sharing and retention?
questions.expectedPractice: You write down who may use the data and how, the conditions for sharing it with partners, where it is stored, how long it is kept, how it is deleted and who decides, by role. In proportion to the risk, this can be a section of the data management plan.
questions.whyAsked: Data that nobody governs drifts into copies on laptops and shared drives, outside the protections the people in it were promised and the project's agreements.
evidenceExamples: the data management plan
a data-sharing or data-access agreement
the storage and access settings, described or linked

answerLabels.not_applicable: We hold no data to govern

answerPrompts.done: Say who can use the data, where it is stored, the sharing conditions, how long it is kept and where the rules are written; this prints in the data card. Name people by role, never by name.
answerPrompts.partly: Say which rules are set and which are still open; this prints in the data card. Name people by role, never by name.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say where the data is stored now, who can use it and your plan; this prints in the data card. Name people by role, never by name.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why the project holds no data to govern; this prints in the data card.

questions.text: Have you checked whether your data has enough examples of rare cases and conditions?
questions.expectedPractice: You list the rare cases and conditions the system will meet in use, count each in the data, and record which are too few to learn from and how you handled them, such as collecting more, grouping them or stating them as a limit.
questions.whyAsked: Rare cases, such as a severe illness or an unusual pest, often have the most at stake, and a model that has seen too few of them handles them badly.
evidenceExamples: a count of rare cases in the data
the summary file from a data profiling notebook
a note on the cases stated as limits

answerPrompts.done: Name the rare cases, how many of each the data holds, what you did about those too few and where it is recorded; this prints in the data card and model card.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the rare cases counted so far and those still to count; this prints in the data card and model card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Name the rare cases you expect the system to meet and when you will count them; this prints in the data card and model card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no rare-case check applies to this project; this prints in the data card and model card.

questions.text: Have domain experts reviewed your data's quality and relevance?
questions.expectedPractice: People who know the field, such as clinicians, agronomists or teachers, review a sample of the data and labels for errors and meaning lost in recording, and you record what they found and what you changed.
questions.whyAsked: Domain experts notice errors that code checks miss, such as a diagnosis code used differently at one clinic, and often find them most cheaply.
evidenceExamples: notes from the expert review
a list of corrections made after the review
terms of reference for the reviewers

answerPrompts.done: Say who reviewed the data, by role, what they looked at and found, what changed and where it is recorded; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.partly: Say who reviewed which part, by role, and what is still to review; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say which experts you plan to involve, by role, and when; this prints in the data card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no domain expertise applies to this data; this prints in the data card.

modules.title: Model Development & Training
modules.description: Assess how the model was selected, designed, and trained.

questions.text: Have you recorded why this type of model suits your problem and data?
questions.expectedPractice: You record the model types you considered, why the chosen one fits the problem, the data and the people who must understand or maintain it, and what you gave up by choosing it.
questions.whyAsked: A model chosen by habit can be harder to explain and maintain than the problem needs; a written choice tells later users what it is for.
evidenceExamples: the model choice note
the methods section of the protocol
a comparison table of candidate models

answerLabels.partly: Partly, some of it is recorded
answerLabels.not_applicable: No choice of model type applies

answerPrompts.done: Name the model type, the alternatives, why you chose it and where this is recorded; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the model type and the alternatives weighed so far, then what is still open; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Name the model type you expect and when you will record the choice; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no choice of model type applies to this project; this prints in the model card.

questions.text: Have you checked that your training, validation and test sets come from the same population?
questions.expectedPractice: You split the data into training, validation and test sets so no person, household or site is in more than one where that would leak information, check they come from the same population, and record how the test set differs from the setting of use.
questions.whyAsked: Test data that overlaps the training data, or comes from another population, makes reported performance wrong in ways nobody sees until the system is in use.
evidenceExamples: the data split code or its description
a table comparing the sets by group and source
the evaluation section of the protocol

answerPrompts.done: Say how you split and checked the sets, how the test data differs from the setting of use and where this is recorded; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.partly: Say how you split the data, which checks are done and which are not, and how the test data differs from the setting of use; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say how and when you plan to split and check the data; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no data split applies to this project; this prints in the model card.

questions.text: Have you measured the kinds of error your model makes, for example with a confusion matrix, precision, recall, specificity and F1?
questions.expectedPractice: On held-out test data, you report the confusion matrix and the measures that matter for your use, such as precision, recall, specificity and F1, and record which error costs the people affected more, and so which measure you watch most.
questions.whyAsked: Accuracy alone can hide a model that misses most cases that matter, and whether a missed case or a false alarm is worse depends on the use.
evidenceExamples: the evaluation report with the confusion matrix
the summary file from the evaluation notebook
a link to the measures in the repository

answerPrompts.done: Name the measures, why those, and the costliest error; give numbers, not judgements. Attach the results file: the model card lists it, and you type the numbers in when you generate it.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the measures reported so far and those still to do; give numbers, not judgements.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you will measure the errors on held-out data, or what is blocking it.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no error measurement applies to this project; this prints in the model card.

questions.text: Have you measured performance separately for each relevant group, for example by age, gender or ethnicity?
questions.expectedPractice: You report the model's main measures separately for each group that matters where it is used, such as sex, age group, district, language, or rural and urban, including groups the data under-represents. Each result gives its number of cases, and you name groups too small for a reliable estimate rather than leave them out.
questions.whyAsked: A model can look good on average and still work badly for one group, whose people carry the cost of its errors.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-14 notebook
a per-group measures table with group sizes

answerPrompts.done: Name the groups, why those, the smallest group's size and where the results are. Type them into the model card when you generate it; the platform does not compute them.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the groups measured so far and those still to do; the platform does not compute them. Collect no new sensitive attribute, such as ethnicity, just for this without consent (see Q-PP-13).
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say which groups you plan and when. Collect no new sensitive attribute, such as ethnicity, just for this without consent (see Q-PP-13).
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no measurement by group applies to this project; this prints in the model card.

questions.text: Which fairness measures have you computed?
questions.expectedPractice: You choose the fairness measures that fit how your system's errors affect people, compute them for the groups you compare and record why those. Most systems that predict something about people need an error-rate measure and a calibration or precision measure. You explain each unticked measure as not fitting and name any fitting measure not listed.
questions.whyAsked: Fairness measures answer different questions and cannot all hold at once, so a result means something only if the measures fit the use and you say why.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-13 notebook
a fairness report with the measures by group
the decision note on which measures fit

answerLabels.done: Every measure that fits our use
answerLabels.partly: Some of the measures that fit

answerPrompts.done: Say why the ticked measures fit, the threshold for each, the groups compared, why each unticked one does not fit and where the report is; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.partly: Say which fitting measures you computed, with thresholds and groups, which are still to compute and why any other does not fit; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Write that no fairness measure is computed yet, which you plan and when; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no fairness measure applies to this project; this prints in the model card.

questions.text: Have you used explanation methods, such as SHAP, LIME or feature importance, to understand your model?
questions.expectedPractice: You apply at least one explanation method that fits your model, such as feature importance, SHAP or LIME, ask people who know the field whether the main drivers of predictions make sense, and record the findings, including any driver that should not matter.
questions.whyAsked: Explanations show whether a model relies on what it should; a driver that makes no sense to a domain expert often first signals a data problem.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-18 notebook
an explanation report with its plots
notes from the expert review of the drivers

answerLabels.partly: Partly, some of it so far

answerPrompts.done: Name the method, the main drivers, the domain expert who reviewed them, by role, their conclusion and where it is recorded.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the method used and the drivers found so far, and what is still to do, such as the expert review.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you will apply an explanation method, or what is blocking it.

questions.text: Have you tested the model on data unlike its training data, such as noisy, incomplete or unusual inputs?
questions.expectedPractice: You test the model on inputs that differ from its training data in the ways expected in use, such as added noise, missing or wrong values, rare cases, lower image or sound quality, and other dialects, devices or sites, with methods such as perturbation tests, held-out sites or the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox. questions.whyAsked: Field data is noisier than training data, so a model never tested on worse inputs can lose much of its accuracy in use without warning.

questions.text: Have you compared your model with a simple baseline such as majority class or logistic regression?
questions.expectedPractice: On the same test data, you compare your model with at least one simple baseline, such as always predicting the most common class, the current rule or a logistic regression, and record whether the gain justifies the complexity.
questions.whyAsked: A complex model barely beating a simple rule costs more to run and explain for little gain; a baseline shows if its numbers mean anything.
evidenceExamples: the evaluation report with the baseline results

questions.text: Have you checked whether the model relies on shortcuts in the data that will not hold in use?
questions.expectedPractice: You look for features that only happen to go with the outcome in your data, such as source site, a watermark or recording time, check whether the model relies on them through explanations, tests on data from other sources or removing the suspect feature, and record what you found.
questions.whyAsked: A shortcut in the data can make a model look good in testing but not in use, and it stays invisible until someone looks for it.

answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no shortcut check applies to this project.

questions.expectedPractice: You check whether the model's stated confidence matches how often it is right, for example with a calibration plot on test data, correct it if needed, and record how users should treat low-confidence outputs.
questions.whyAsked: Users act on stated confidence, so a model that is confidently wrong is more dangerous than one that says it is unsure.

modules.title: Evaluation, Fairness & Documentation
modules.description: Assess model evaluation rigor, fairness analysis, and documentation practices.

questions.text: Have you chosen the simplest model that performs well enough?
questions.expectedPractice: You define acceptable performance for this use, then choose the simplest model that reaches it, weighing how far those affected and those acting on outputs need to understand each decision, and record the choice and trade-offs.
questions.whyAsked: Simpler models are easier to explain, check and maintain, which matters most where people must understand decisions about them; small accuracy gains may not be worth it.

questions.text: Have you recorded what you need to retrain the same model: settings, random seeds, code and software versions?
questions.expectedPractice: You keep with the model what is needed to re-run training and get the same model: code and data versions, preprocessing steps, settings including hyperparameters and random seeds, and software versions.

questions.text: Have you checked that your data pipeline does not lose or change records?
questions.expectedPractice: You add checks, such as row counts, value ranges, units, date formats and the character encoding of local languages, at each step of your data pipeline to catch lost, duplicated or changed records, and record what they find.

questions.text: Which other evaluation methods have you used?
questions.expectedPractice: You use the evaluation methods your model and data need for stable, honest estimates and record what each showed: for most projects cross-validation or bootstrapping, error analysis by subgroup and a sensitivity analysis; calibration and AUC-ROC where the model gives probabilities. You explain unticked methods as not relevant.

questions.text: Have you checked whether pooling data across populations hides important differences between them?
questions.expectedPractice: You compare results for the main subpopulations you pooled, such as regions, languages or types of facility, check whether pooled results hide opposite trends within them, and record whether one model serves all or separate handling is needed.

questions.text: When you tuned the model's settings, such as the decision threshold, did you check that results did not get worse for some groups?
questions.expectedPractice: You check whether your tuning choices, such as the decision threshold, class weights and the measure you optimised, made results worse for some groups, by comparing results by group before and after tuning, and record the changes you made.
questions.whyAsked: Tuning for the best overall result often favours the largest group, and a threshold set on the whole population can leave a smaller group with far more missed cases.

questions.expectedPractice: You describe what each kind of error means for those affected, such as a missed diagnosis or a service wrongly refused, compare error rates across groups, and record which groups bear more harm and your response.

answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no harm-by-group assessment applies to this project; this prints in the model card.

questions.text: Have you recorded the model's known limits, the ways it goes wrong and the conditions where it must not be used?
questions.expectedPractice: You record where the model is known to perform poorly or was not tested, by population, place, device, language and time period, the kinds of errors it makes and the situations where it must not be used. You write it for those who will deploy or rely on the model and keep it with the model.

questions.text: Have you used version control for your code, data processing and trained models?
questions.expectedPractice: You keep code, data processing and trained models under version control (for example Git for code, DVC or MLflow for data and models), so each model in use traces to the code and data that made it.
questions.whyAsked: Without versions, nobody can trace the model in use to its code and data, which is how you find the cause when something goes wrong.

questions.expectedPractice: In proportion to the risk of misuse, you consider how someone could trick or manipulate the model, such as with altered images, reworded text or fake inputs, test the likeliest ways, by hand or with the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox, and record the results and safeguards chosen.

questions.text: Have you tested the model on data from after its training period?

modules.title: Deployment & Monitoring
modules.description: Assess deployment plans, monitoring capabilities, and operational safeguards.

questions.text: Once your system is in use, do you regularly check whether its inputs or its performance have changed?
questions.expectedPractice: Once the system is in use, a named person checks on a set schedule whether its inputs and its performance have moved away from what it was tested on. You record the checks, their thresholds and who acts when a threshold is crossed.

questions.expectedPractice: You have a written plan for when the system causes or may cause harm. It says how a problem is reported, who is alerted, by role, how the system is paused or limited, how the people affected are told and helped, and how the cause is found and fixed.

questions.expectedPractice: You check results for each place, language and kind of user the system serves, such as districts, dialects, devices or literacy, and record where it works less well and what you did.
questions.whyAsked: A system tested in one place or language often works worse in another; users there carry the cost unless someone checks.
evidenceExamples: results by setting
notes from field testing at different sites
results of testing with users in each language

answerPrompts.done: Name the settings compared, what you found, what you changed or stated as a limit, and where it is recorded.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the settings compared so far and what you found, then those still to compare.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say which settings you plan to compare and when, or what is blocking it.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no check by setting applies to this project.

questions.text: Have you planned when and how your system will be retired or replaced?
questions.expectedPractice: You record when the system should be retired or replaced, such as when the need ends, a better method exists or upkeep costs too much, and how: who decides, how users and data are handled, and what replaces it. The plan counts the computing and energy the system uses while running, estimated from hardware hours and power draw.
questions.whyAsked: Systems left running after their purpose ends keep using money and power and drift without oversight; planning the end at the start means someone decides when to stop.
evidenceExamples: the retirement section of the deployment plan
the running cost estimate, with energy

answerPrompts.done: Say what would trigger retirement, who decides, by role, your estimate of computing and energy while running, and where the plan is kept.
answerPrompts.partly: Say which parts of the plan exist, such as the triggers or the energy estimate, and which are missing.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you will plan the end of the system, or what is blocking it.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no retirement plan applies to this project.

questions.text: Does your system handle unusual inputs safely, such as by flagging them for a person rather than giving a confident answer?
questions.expectedPractice: Your system detects inputs unlike those it was built on, such as by checking value ranges or the model's confidence, and handles them safely: it flags them, asks a person to decide or falls back to the earlier practice. You tested this and record how it works.
questions.whyAsked: Every system meets inputs it was not built for; a safe one flags them for a person to decide instead of giving a confident wrong answer.
evidenceExamples: the design note on handling unusual inputs
test results with unusual inputs
the fallback procedure

answerPrompts.done: Say how unusual inputs are detected, what the system then does, how you tested it and where this is recorded.
answerPrompts.partly: Say which unusual inputs are detected and handled so far, and which are not.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say how and when you plan to detect and handle unusual inputs.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no unusual-input handling applies to this project.

questions.text: Have you told all stakeholders what your system is for and its limits?
questions.expectedPractice: You tell the people who decide on, run or rely on the system, in writing and in their language, what it is for, where it may not be used and its main limits, and record who was told, by role. How each output is shown to users is a separate question.
questions.whyAsked: Limits that only the build team knows protect nobody; decision-makers and partners need them in writing before they rely on the system.
evidenceExamples: the briefing note to partners
the model card or its limitations section
minutes of the handover meeting

answerLabels.not_applicable: No briefing on use and limits applies

answerPrompts.done: Give the intended use and main limits first, then who was told, by role or organisation, how, and where it is recorded; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.partly: Give the intended use and main limits first, then who has been told so far and who not, by role or organisation; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Give the intended use and main limits first, then when and how you will tell people; this prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Give the intended use and main limits first, then say why no briefing on use and limits applies to this project; this prints in the model card.

questions.text: Have representatives of the affected communities helped design and evaluate your system?
questions.expectedPractice: Representatives of the affected communities help design and evaluate the system, such as in a community advisory group or review sessions; you record their input, by role or group, and what it changed.
questions.whyAsked: Communities know what will help or harm them as a project team cannot; their review checks your blind spots from outside.
evidenceExamples: notes from community review sessions
the terms of reference of a community advisory group
a note of the changes made after their input

answerLabels.partly: Partly, in some of the work

answerPrompts.done: Say who took part, by group or role, how and when, and what you changed; link the notes, never a participant list.
answerPrompts.partly: Say who has taken part so far, by group or role, and where not yet; upload no participant list.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say which communities you plan to involve, how and when.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no community input applies to this project.

questions.text: Have you checked how your system changes existing workflows and professional practice?
questions.expectedPractice: You look at how the system changes its users' work, such as extra steps, time and responsibilities, try it in the real workflow, and record the problems found and what you changed.
questions.whyAsked: A system that adds work or confusion is used badly or not at all, and staff may rely on it in unplanned ways.
evidenceExamples: notes from a trial in the workflow
feedback from users, by role
the updated workflow description

answerLabels.partly: Partly, for some of the work

answerPrompts.done: Say what workflow changes you found and how, naming staff by role, what you changed and where it is recorded.
answerPrompts.partly: Say which parts of the workflow you have looked at so far and what is still open.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you will try the system in the real workflow, or what is blocking it.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no workflow check applies to this project.

questions.text: Have you identified the data protection and ethics rules that apply and obtained the approvals and registrations they require?
questions.expectedPractice: You identify which data-protection, research-ethics and sector rules apply where the system is built and where it is used, such as the national data protection law and the national research ethics guidelines of each country concerned. You obtain the approvals and registrations they require and record each with its reference and date.
questions.whyAsked: Approvals are easy to lose track of when research moves into use; a missing one can stop a deployment and expose the people whose data is used.
evidenceExamples: approval letters
registration documents
a data protection impact assessment
a note from the institution's data protection officer

answerLabels.partly: Partly, some of it in place

answerPrompts.done: List each rule and its approval or registration: body, reference and date; attach the letters. The platform records your statement and makes no judgement of it.
answerPrompts.partly: List each rule, the approvals held with body, reference and date, and those you still wait for. The platform makes no judgement of your statement.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you will identify the rules that apply, or what is blocking it.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no data protection, research ethics or sector rule applies to this project; the platform makes no judgement of your statement.

questions.text: Do you regularly review your system's performance and whether it should still be used?
questions.expectedPractice: On a set schedule, in proportion to the risk, you review performance, results by group, user feedback and whether the system is still needed, and record and act on the decisions.
questions.whyAsked: Monitoring watches the numbers; only a review on a set date asks whether the system should still be used as it is.
evidenceExamples: the review schedule
minutes of the last review
the decision record of a review

answerPrompts.done: Give how often you review, who takes part, by role, and the last review's date and decision; link its minutes.
answerPrompts.partly: Say what your reviews cover so far, how often they happen, and what is missing.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when the first review will be and who will take part, by role.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no regular review applies to this project.

questions.text: Have you checked whether people with less access can reach and use your system?
questions.expectedPractice: You check whether people with less access, such as those with older phones, poor connectivity, low literacy or another language, can reach and use the system, and record any gap and your response.
questions.whyAsked: A service run through an AI system can leave out those who need it most; checking access shows who is left behind.
evidenceExamples: results of testing on basic phones or offline
notes from users with limited access
a note on the changes made

answerPrompts.done: Name the groups checked, what you found and changed, and where it is recorded.
answerPrompts.partly: Name the groups checked so far, what you found, and those still to check.
answerPrompts.not_yet: Say which groups you plan to check and when, or what is blocking it.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no access check applies to this project.
